Safe driving is not only about knowing traffic rules. It also requires understanding how speed, reaction time, grip, visibility, fatigue and vehicle condition affect the time and space needed to avoid a collision.

This chapter combines practical road-safety principles with the Dutch legal rules that matter most. Where a figure is only a rule of thumb rather than a statutory limit, it is identified as such.

Stopping Distance

Reaction distance plus braking distance — and why there is no single fixed braking-distance formula for every car and road.

From Seeing a Hazard to Coming to a Stop

Before a vehicle stops, two distances matter:

  • Reaction distance: the distance travelled while the driver notices the hazard, decides what to do and begins braking.
  • Braking distance: the distance travelled from the start of effective braking until the vehicle comes to rest.

Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance. Reaction time varies with alertness, distraction, fatigue, alcohol, drugs and medication. Braking distance varies with speed, tyres, brakes, road grip, gradient, vehicle load and other conditions.

Reaction-Distance Estimate
speed in km/h ÷ 3.6 × reaction time in seconds
For a simple one-second reaction-time example, divide the speed by 3.6. This is an illustration, not a legal formula and not a guarantee of actual stopping distance.

Speed Has a Squared Effect on Braking Distance Core physics

Under otherwise similar conditions, braking distance increases roughly with the square of speed. Doubling speed therefore requires about four times the braking distance — not twice the distance.

This square relationship applies to the braking part of the stop. Total stopping distance also includes reaction distance, which increases approximately in direct proportion to speed for the same reaction time.

What Makes Stopping Distance Longer? Conditions matter

There is no universal rule that a wet road always doubles stopping distance or that ice always multiplies it by exactly ten. The real increase depends on grip and vehicle conditions. Important factors include:

  • Wet, snowy or icy surfaces: available tyre grip can fall sharply.
  • Worn or damaged tyres: less grip and greater aquaplaning risk.
  • Brake defects or poor maintenance: reduced braking performance.
  • Fatigue, alcohol, drugs, medication or distraction: longer reaction time before braking begins.
  • Downhill gradients: more distance may be needed to reduce speed or stop.
  • Heavy loads or trailers: handling and braking performance can change significantly.

Following Distance

Leave enough space to react, brake and still avoid the vehicle ahead.

The Two-Second Rule Practical rule of thumb

A widely used practical method is to keep at least a two-second gap in good conditions. When the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point, count two seconds; you should not reach that point before the count is complete.

The two-second figure is a safety rule of thumb, not a numerical distance written into Article 19 of the RVV. The legal principle is broader: you must be able to stop within the distance you can see to be clear. At 120 km/h, two seconds corresponds to about 67 metres.

Increase the Gap When Conditions Worsen More time, more space

Two seconds is only a practical starting point for good conditions. Increase the gap when grip, visibility or reaction ability is worse, for example:

  • Rain or a wet road: leave substantially more room because grip and visibility are reduced.
  • Snow, frost or ice: use a much larger margin and very gentle control inputs.
  • Fog or darkness: choose a speed and gap that allow you to stop within the distance you can see to be clear.
  • Behind a large vehicle: extra space improves your view ahead and gives more time to react.
  • With a trailer or heavy load: allow for changed braking and handling.
  • When tired or distracted: do not rely on extra distance as a cure; reduce risk and stop if you are not fit to continue safely.
Tailgating Leaves Too Little Time to React

A short gap removes the safety margin needed when traffic ahead brakes suddenly. Article 19 RVV requires a driver to be able to stop within the distance over which the road can be seen to be clear. Keep a larger gap whenever the situation makes stopping more difficult.

Visibility & Vision

Seeing far enough to stop safely — and using lights correctly so others can see you.

Article 19: Stop Within the Distance You Can See to Be Clear Legal rule

Article 19 RVV requires the driver to be able to bring the vehicle to a stop within the distance over which the road can be seen and is clear. That principle applies in fog, rain, snow, darkness, bends and any other situation with restricted sight distance.

The posted speed limit is a maximum, not a guarantee that the speed is safe. When visibility or grip is poor, the safe speed can be well below the posted limit.

🌫️ Fog

Reduce speed and increase the gap. Front fog lights may be used when fog, snowfall or rain seriously impairs visibility. A rear fog light may be used only in fog or snowfall when visibility is less than 50 metres — not simply because it is raining.

🌧️ Rain

Rain reduces visibility and grip and can create spray. Use dipped headlights when visibility is seriously impaired, reduce speed and leave more following distance.

☀️ Low sun

Low sun can temporarily reduce vision. Keep the windscreen clean, use the sun visor or suitable sunglasses and reduce speed when glare limits what you can see.

🌙 Night driving

Dipped headlights are required at night. Main beam may be used instead where permitted, but not during the day, when meeting another road user, or when following another vehicle at short distance. Adjust speed to the distance illuminated and visible ahead.

🚛 Behind a large vehicle

A truck or bus can block your view of traffic ahead. Leave extra space so you can see more of the road and react earlier to changing traffic.

↪️ Blind bends

Approach at a speed that allows you to stop within the part of the road you can see to be clear. Do not begin an overtaking manoeuvre when you cannot see enough clear road ahead.

Being Seen by Others Lights and warnings

Use the legally required lighting for the conditions and remember that daytime-running lights do not necessarily illuminate the rear of every vehicle. At night and when daytime visibility is seriously impaired, use dipped headlights unless another permitted lighting rule applies.

If a stationary vehicle forms an obstacle, approaching traffic must be warned in time. In the Netherlands this can be done with hazard warning lights or a warning triangle. The triangle is not compulsory equipment, and when the hazard warning lights are operating a triangle is not required. If used, it is placed about 30 metres behind the vehicle.

A high-visibility vest is sensible emergency equipment, but it is not compulsory to carry or wear one in the Netherlands.

Skidding & Loss of Control

Prevent loss of grip first; if it happens, keep every input smooth and avoid panic corrections.

Why a Vehicle Skids Available grip exceeded

A skid occurs when the tyre is asked to provide more braking, acceleration or cornering force than the available grip can support. Common triggers include:

  • Excessive braking: wheel lock on a non-ABS vehicle removes much of the ability to steer.
  • Excessive acceleration: driven wheels can spin when grip is poor.
  • Too much speed in a bend: the vehicle can run wide (understeer) or the rear can step outward (oversteer).
  • Abrupt steering or throttle changes: sudden inputs can destabilise the vehicle, especially on slippery surfaces.
Preventing Skids Smooth inputs
  • Reduce speed before the bend: enter at a speed that leaves grip available for steering.
  • Brake progressively: avoid unnecessary abrupt braking; if an emergency stop is required in an ABS-equipped car, apply firm continuous pressure.
  • Accelerate smoothly: especially on wet, icy or loose surfaces.
  • Increase your safety margin: leave more space so you do not need sudden braking or steering.
  • Maintain the tyres: correct pressure, sufficient tread and no serious damage are essential for grip.
If Grip Is Lost Stay smooth

The exact response depends on the vehicle, tyres, road surface and whether the front or rear tyres have lost grip. General principles are:

  • Look where you want the vehicle to go and avoid sudden steering corrections.
  • Ease off the accelerator smoothly unless power is specifically needed to stabilise the vehicle.
  • Understeer: reduce speed smoothly and avoid adding more steering lock; the tyres need grip before the car can turn more sharply.
  • Oversteer: correct the steering smoothly toward the direction of the slide and avoid over-correcting.
  • ABS emergency braking: press the brake firmly and continuously and steer as needed; do not pump the pedal.
ABS — Anti-lock Braking System

ABS prevents the wheels from remaining locked during heavy braking, helping the driver retain steering control. In an emergency stop with ABS, press the brake pedal firmly and keep pressure on it while steering around a hazard if necessary. Pedal vibration or noise can be normal. ABS does not guarantee the shortest possible stopping distance on every surface; its major safety advantage is preserving wheel rotation and steering control.

Fatigue & Attention

Tired drivers react more slowly, concentrate less effectively and can fall asleep without warning.

Fatigue Seriously Reduces Driving Performance Stop before microsleep

Fatigue reduces attention, reaction speed, lane keeping and hazard perception. Research often compares severe sleep deprivation with alcohol-like impairment, but those comparisons are approximate research findings — they are not legal alcohol equivalents.

The greatest danger is microsleep: a driver can lose awareness for several seconds and travel a long distance without meaningful control. If you are struggling to stay awake, continuing to drive is unsafe.

Warning Signs of Dangerous Fatigue Act early
  • Difficulty keeping your eyes open or your head upright.
  • Repeated yawning and trouble concentrating.
  • Drifting within or across the lane.
  • Missing signs, exits or junctions.
  • Not remembering the last part of the journey.
  • Brief involuntary lapses of awareness or microsleeps.
Opening a window, turning up music or relying on willpower does not restore alertness. Stop in a safe place and rest. If you are very sleepy, a short nap is more effective than trying to push on.
Managing Fatigue on Long Journeys Plan breaks
  • Start a long journey well rested.
  • Plan regular breaks; a common road-safety recommendation is to stop after about two hours of driving and rest for roughly 15 minutes.
  • Avoid driving through the hours when you would normally be asleep whenever possible.
  • If drowsiness develops, stop somewhere safe. A short nap can restore alertness temporarily; caffeine may help for a while but is not a substitute for sleep.
  • Share driving on long journeys if another qualified and rested driver is available.

Vehicle Condition

A vehicle used on the road must meet the applicable technical requirements; safety checks remain important between APK inspections.

Roadworthiness Is More Than the APK Regeling voertuigen

Vehicles used on public roads must comply with the applicable permanent technical requirements in the Regeling voertuigen. The APK is a periodic inspection, not a guarantee that the vehicle will remain safe until the next inspection.

If a defect makes the vehicle unsafe or causes it no longer to meet the legal requirements, it must be repaired before normal use. Responsibility and liability after an incident depend on the defect, the driver's knowledge and the circumstances; they are not automatically identical in every case.

🔵 Tyres

For passenger cars, the main tread grooves must have at least 1.6 mm tread depth around the full circumference of the tread. Tyres must not expose the carcass or have prohibited bulges. Check pressure and visible damage regularly.

🔴 Brakes

Brakes must meet the technical requirements and operate effectively. Unusual noises, pulling, vibration, warning lights or a major change in pedal feel are reasons to have the system inspected promptly.

💡 Lights

Required lights must be present and work correctly. Check dipped beam, rear lights, brake lights, indicators and other required lighting before relying on the vehicle in darkness or poor visibility.

🔧 Steering

Unexpected play, vibration, pulling or unusual steering effort can indicate a fault. Have significant changes investigated before they develop into a loss-of-control risk.

🪟 Windows & mirrors

The driver must have adequate visibility. Required mirrors must be usable, and the windscreen and relevant side windows must meet the legal requirements on visibility, damage and obstruction. Demist or de-ice the windscreen sufficiently before moving.

📋 APK

APK frequency depends on vehicle age, fuel type and vehicle category. For many petrol, alcohol or electric passenger cars under 30 years old, the pattern is first inspection at 4 years, then twice at 2-year intervals, then annually. Many diesel or gas cars are inspected first at 3 years and then annually. Check the exact expiry date in the RDW register or on the APK report — there is no general Dutch APK windscreen-sticker system.

Quick Pre-Drive Check

Before a long journey, take a minute to check the tyres, lights, mirrors and windows, dashboard warning lights, fuel or battery range, and any obvious leaks or damage. If braking or steering feels abnormal, do not treat a recently passed APK as proof that the vehicle is safe to continue driving.

Road & Weather Conditions

Grip and visibility can change quickly; adapt speed, following distance and control inputs to the conditions.

ConditionWhat changesMain riskSafer response
Dry roadBest normal gripOverconfidence / excessive speedMaintain a safe gap and stay within the legal and safe speed for the situation.
Wet roadGrip and visibility are reducedLonger stopping distance and aquaplaningReduce speed, increase following distance and use appropriate lighting.
AquaplaningTyres lose effective contact with the roadSteering and braking response falls sharplyEase off the accelerator smoothly and avoid abrupt braking or steering until grip returns.
SnowGrip can be very lowWheelspin, skidding and long stopping distanceUse very low speeds and large margins. Winter tyres are not compulsory in the Netherlands but can improve grip in winter conditions.
Ice / black iceGrip can become extremely lowLoss of control with little warningUse very gentle steering, braking and acceleration; reduce speed before the slippery section.
FogVisibility can collapse rapidlyDriving faster than the visible stopping distanceReduce speed, increase the gap and use lights according to the RVV fog-light rules.
CrosswindVehicle can be pushed sidewaysSudden lane movement, especially for tall vehicles or trailersReduce speed if necessary, hold the steering steadily and expect gusts near open areas, bridges and when passing large vehicles.
Low sun / glareForward vision is reducedLate detection of traffic and signalsKeep glass clean, use the visor or suitable sunglasses and reduce speed.
Wet leavesSurface grip can dropSkidding under braking or corneringReduce speed and avoid abrupt control inputs.
Aquaplaning — What It Is and What to Do Loss of tyre contact

Aquaplaning occurs when water builds up between the tyres and the road faster than the tread can disperse it. Steering can suddenly feel light and the vehicle may stop responding normally to steering or braking.

What to do: ease off the accelerator smoothly, keep the steering as steady as possible and avoid sudden braking or sharp steering. Let the vehicle slow until the tyres regain effective contact, then correct your path smoothly.

Aquaplaning risk generally rises with speed and standing water, and it increases when tyre tread is worn or tyre condition is poor.
Winter Driving in the Netherlands Know the Dutch rules

Winter tyres are not legally mandatory in the Netherlands, although they can provide better grip in winter conditions, especially on snow. Snow chains, by contrast, may not normally be used on Dutch public roads because they can damage the road surface; exceptional permission can be possible in individual cases.

Before driving in winter conditions:

  • Clear enough snow, ice and condensation from windows, mirrors and lights to maintain proper visibility and signalling.
  • Remove loose snow or ice that could create a hazard for other road users.
  • Check tyre condition and pressure.
  • Allow more time and avoid abrupt braking, steering and acceleration.
  • Carry sensible emergency supplies for a long journey, especially in very cold weather.
Chapter 9 — What to Take Away

Stopping distance is reaction distance plus braking distance; braking distance rises sharply with speed. Following distance: two seconds is a useful rule of thumb in good conditions, not a fixed legal minimum. Article 19: you must be able to stop within the distance you can see to be clear. Visibility: use dipped, main and fog lights according to the RVV rules. Fatigue: stop and rest when alertness falls. Vehicle condition: the APK does not replace day-to-day responsibility for a roadworthy vehicle. Winter: winter tyres are optional in the Netherlands; snow chains are generally prohibited on public roads.
